chunks: What a multiphase buck is. The question: What is a multiphase buck converter?
A multiphase buck is several small buck converters, called phases, that share one output and one load. Each phase has its own inductor and its own pair of switches.
They take turns: each starts its cycle a fraction of a period after the one before. The load sees the combined current, which is bigger and smoother than any one phase could give.
Think of a car engine. One huge cylinder firing once per turn would shake the whole engine. Four smaller cylinders firing in turn give smooth, steady power.
In a multiphase buck, each phase is one cylinder. Their pulses interleave so the gaps in one are filled by another.
The analogy does not show the downside: the "cylinders" must be balanced or one of them does too much of the work.
Two phases shown. Each phase is a half-bridge (HS, LS) feeding its own inductor from its own switch node (SW1, SW2).
Both inductors land on the same output node and share C out and the load. Add more columns for more phases; the controller, not the schematic, is what makes them take turns.
Phase: one complete buck stage, with its own inductor and its own pair of switches (FETs) ("How a buck converter works").
Interleaving: starting the phases at evenly spaced times, 1 over N of a period apart. Ripple cancellation: the phases' up-and-down currents partly offset each other at the output.
Phase count ( N ): how many phases are in parallel. Current balancing: making the phases share the load equally.
A processor's supply needs 60 amps. Four phases each carry about 15 amps, which is a manageable load for each stage.
If each phase switches at 500 kilohertz, the four are offset by a quarter of a period, so a new pulse arrives every 1 over (4 times 500 k ) equals 0. 5 microseconds.
The output capacitor therefore sees ripple at 2 megahertz, four times the per-phase rate. That is the whole idea.
"A multiphase buck is N buck power stages that share one output capacitor and one load but switch at evenly staggered times, 360 over N degrees apart.
Each phase carries about one N-th of the current.
The inductor currents add at the output and their ripples partly cancel, so the capacitor sees much less ripple, at N times the switching frequency.
That lets you deliver high current, respond quickly to load steps and spread the heat, which is why CPU and GPU core rails are built this way."
